To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the time-resolved spectra of PS II are reproduced well by the simulations based on a refined set of excitonic couplings and site energies of the chlorophylls, that the 695 nm fluorescence is assigned to a red-shifted chlorin pool in CP47, and that the 685 nm fluorescence is assigned either to Chl45 in CP43 or to Chl43 in the same protein.

the time-resolved and stationary optical spectra of photosystem two (PSII) are well reproduced by a theoretical model that treats the excitonic couplings of the pigment-protein complexes by a quantum chemical method and the exciton dynamics by the Redfield and generalized Förster theories.

(a) PS II does not possess a simple excitation energy funnel, (b) exciton dynamics is a key element in the understanding of the fluorescence properties of PS II, (c) the 695 nm emitting pool of chlorophyll is located in CP47 and might be involved in photoregulation, and (d) PS II-CC is an excellent model system for the study of exciton dynamics in photosynthesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a theoretical model of the excitation energy transfer dynamics of PS II, which is capable of explaining the experimentally observed time-resolved fluorescence properties.
the elucidation of the structure and dynamics of the primary light reactions in the photosynthetic apparatus of oxygenic photosynthesis.
the development of a comprehensive model for the description of the optical spectra of PSII-CC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fluorescence spectrum of PSII-CC at low temperature is a result of excitons trapped by two red-shifted pigments, which are Chl45/Chl43 and Chl29 in PSII-CC, respectively.
the PS II-CC does not possess a simple excitation energy funnel.
PS II-CC possesses an excitonic energy funnel with an entrance and an exit, but not a simple one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the time-resolved and stationary fluorescence spectra of PS II are reproduced well by the excitonic model, which is based on the quantum chemical/electronic structure calculation and Redfield theory, and thus the excitonic couplings and the relaxation processes are not too far from the simple picture.

the fluorescence spectra of PS II-PC at low temperatures are reproduced well by our model calculations, which are based on the excitonic coupling of pigments calculated by a quantum chemistry/electrostatics method.

the PS II core complex possesses a rather complicated excitonic structure, in which the exciton dynamics are strongly influenced by temperature and the existence of two distinct red-shifted chlorophy1l pools.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PS II-CC is not a simple energy funnel.

the time-resolved spectra of PS II- CC cannot be understood in the framework of the conventional model, in which excitations are assumed to be delocalized on the order of 20 chlorophylls and to be trapped at a single chlorophyll in the Q _{A} site.
the time-resolved spectra of PS II- CC are well reproduced by a model that assumes the presence of exciton domains.
